card.name: Gambuh
card.tagline: An ancient, technically demanding Balinese dance-drama from the 15th-century Majapahit era.
card.profile: Gambuh is an ancient Balinese dance-drama originating in the 15th-century Majapahit era. Once supported by royal courts, it now survives primarily in the village of Batuan. It is considered the foundation for many other Balinese performing arts, including topeng and arja. The performance combines complex music, Kawi language dialogue, and refined movement to enact the Malat epic.
card.insight: Gambuh is the source of all classical Balinese dance, yet it is so rare that only four groups were recorded performing it in 1997, largely due to the extreme complexity of its music and Kawi language dialogue.

card.profile_long: Gambuh is one of the oldest surviving forms of Balinese performing arts, with roots tracing back to the late Majapahit era in the 15th century. Historically, it served as a sophisticated court art, sustained by the patronage of the Balinese aristocracy. Following the collapse of these courts during conflicts with the Dutch, the tradition faced a decline in support, leading to the loss of much of its repertoire. Today, the form is preserved primarily in the village of Batuan, with very few active performance groups remaining. It is recognized as the source of all classical Balinese dance, having introduced narrative structures that influenced later forms such as the topeng masked dance and arja opera. The performance is technically demanding, requiring performers to master the archaic Kawi language and musicians to play specialized, long bamboo flutes. Because the performances are lengthy and lack significant comic relief, they present a challenge for modern audiences. The narrative content is drawn from the Malat, a series of poems detailing the romance of the fictional Javanese prince Raden Panji and his fiancée, Rangkesari. The story follows their separation, their years of searching across medieval Java, and their eventual reunion on the battlefield. The characters are divided by status, with refined (alus) characters speaking in the literary Kawi tongue, which is then translated into contemporary Balinese by lower-status characters for the audience. The musical accompaniment, known as the gamelan gambuh, is distinct from other Balinese ensembles, incorporating instruments such as the kenyir, kangsi, and gumanak that are not found elsewhere on the island.

sections.origins_and_history: Gambuh dates to the 15th-century Majapahit era. It was historically supported by royal courts until their collapse during wars with the Dutch, after which it shifted toward performance at temple ceremonies.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Technique not described in sources, though it is noted as being the richest in movement of all classical Balinese dance forms.
sections.music_and_instruments: The gamelan gambuh ensemble requires approximately 17 musicians. Key instruments include 75-100 cm bamboo flutes (suling gambuh), a rebab, and unique percussion instruments including the kenyir, kangsi, and gumanak.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performances are held at temple ceremonies and center on the Malat epic, a narrative about Prince Raden Panji and his search for his fiancée.
sections.lineage: Gambuh influenced other Balinese forms including topeng masked dance and arja opera.
